meta.title: Who originally recorded "At Last"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Etta James didn't originate "At Last." Glenn Miller and His Orchestra cut the first released version on May 20, 1942, for RCA Victor.
meta.ogDescription: The wedding-dance standard began as a Glenn Miller B-side, sung by Ray Eberle and recorded in Hollywood on May 20, 1942 for RCA Victor.

answer.label: Not an Etta James original — a 1942 Glenn Miller and His Orchestra single on RCA Victor
answer.originalArtistDates: Formed 1938 · American swing dance band · last civilian concert September 27, 1942
answer.sourceLine: Because Etta James’s Argo recording has become the sound of first dances and awards-show montages, she is widely taken to have originated “At Last.” She did not. Mack Gordon and Harry Warren wrote it for the 1941 film Sun Valley Serenade, and the first commercially released recording is by Glenn Miller and His Orchestra with Ray Eberle singing, cut in Hollywood on May 20, 1942 and issued by RCA Victor. It was not even the plug side: it went out as the B-side of “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo,” and its record label credits a different film again.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: RCA Victor
original.released: Recorded in Hollywood on May 20, 1942 (Victor matrix PBS-072285, take 1 the master) and issued by RCA Victor as a 10-inch 78 rpm single, catalogue 27934. It was the B-side — the A-side was “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo.” The disc label describes it as a fox trot from the 20th Century-Fox picture Orchestra Wives, not from Sun Valley Serenade, the film it was actually written for. The recording was later pressed as a U.S. Army V-Disc, No. 12A, in October 1943.
original.charted: It charted in the US in the summer of 1942, but the peak is reported inconsistently and this page will not pick a winner. Wikipedia’s cited chart data has it entering Billboard’s “Songs with the Most Radio Plugs” listing at number 17 on August 1, 1942 and reaching number two on August 29; other reference sources give markedly lower peaks. Billboard ran several competing listings in 1942 — radio plugs, retail sales, jukebox play — and secondary sources do not agree on which one they are quoting.
original.cover: Etta James recorded it in 1960 in an arrangement by Riley Hampton, as the title track of her debut album At Last!, released November 15, 1960 on Argo Records and produced by Leonard and Phil Chess. As a single it reached number two on Billboard’s R&B chart and crossed to number 47 on the Hot 100 in April 1961. It was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999.

original.trailTitle: How the 1942 date was pinned down
trail: The Discography of American Historical Recordings ↗ reproduces the Victor entry from the company’s own paperwork — it cites the Victor ledgers, the Victor blue history card and the Rigler-Deutsch Index. It logs matrix PBS-072285, recorded May 20, 1942 in Hollywood, take 1 as the master, issued on Victor 27934, with Ray Eberle as vocalist, Glenn Miller directing and Harry Meyerson supervising the session.
MusicBrainz carries the single itself — RCA Victor 27934, dated July 10, 1942 ↗ — with “At Last” as the second side, behind “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo.”

The physical disc survives as a library digitisation: the Internet Archive’s transfer of Victor 27934-B ↗ carries the matrix stamp, a runtime of 3:12, and a label reading “Fox Trot with Vocal Refrain, from the 20th Century-Fox picture Orchestra Wives.”
Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ records the detail that makes the year confusing: Miller’s orchestra made recordings of “At Last” in 1941, and none of them were released.

authors.name: Glenn Miller and His Orchestra
authors.heading: Who actually recorded it first
authors.metaLine: American swing dance band · formed 1938 · last civilian concert September 27, 1942
authors.bio: The most commercially successful dance orchestra of the swing era, built around a clarinet-led reed voicing that made it identifiable in a bar or two. It filmed “At Last” for Sun Valley Serenade in 1941 and recorded it in the studio that year without releasing anything, then cut the version the public finally heard on May 20, 1942 in Hollywood, with Ray Eberle singing and an arrangement by Jerry Gray and Bill Finegan. The timing was tight: the band was near the end of its civilian life, and Miller played his last concert with it in Passaic, New Jersey on September 27, 1942 before going into the Army.

authors.name: Etta James
authors.heading: Who everyone thinks recorded it first
authors.metaLine: 1938–2012 · American blues, R&B and soul singer
authors.bio: Jamesetta Hawkins recorded “At Last” for Argo in 1960, in a Riley Hampton arrangement that kept Warren’s melody but rebuilt everything around it — strings where the brass had been, and a vocal that treats the song as testimony rather than as a dance number. It became the title track of her debut album and, in April 1961, a number two R&B hit that crossed to the pop chart. The credit confusion is chronological only: her record is so completely her own that it is easy to assume nobody had a claim on the song before her.

authors.name: Mack Gordon and Harry Warren
authors.heading: Who wrote it
authors.metaLine: Mack Gordon, 1904–1959, lyricist · Harry Warren, 1893–1981, composer
authors.bio: Warren wrote the music and Gordon the words, working as 20th Century-Fox’s house songwriting team. Warren was the first major American songwriter to work primarily in film and won three Oscars for Best Original Song; Gordon was nominated nine times in eleven years and won once, for “You’ll Never Know,” which the two of them wrote together. “At Last” is among the most durable things either man produced, though neither lived to see the version that made it famous become the standard.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody claims Etta James wrote “At Last” — the Warren and Gordon credit is printed on every release. The slip is a different one: her record is so thoroughly hers that it is routinely treated as the song’s point of origin, the recording everything else descends from. It is a cover, and the thing it covers is a big-band B-side.

items.why: Recorded in 1960 in a Riley Hampton arrangement and released November 15 that year as the title track of At Last!. It reached number two R&B and number 47 on the Hot 100 in April 1961, and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999. Great record, later record.

items.who: Glenn Miller and His Orchestra, vocal by Ray Eberle
items.why: Recorded May 20, 1942 in Hollywood as Victor matrix PBS-072285 and issued on RCA Victor 27934 — as the B-side of “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo.” Miller’s orchestra also recorded the song in 1941, but nothing from those sessions was released.
Written for the 1941 film Sun Valley Serenade, where the vocal was cut before release. Neither man had anything to do with the 1960 record.

The biggest American chart placing for “At Last” belongs to neither Miller nor James. Anthony — a former trumpeter in Miller’s own orchestra — took a remake of it to number two on Billboard’s pop singles chart in 1952.

misattribution.truthLine: Glenn Miller and His Orchestra recorded “At Last” first, in Hollywood on May 20, 1942, with Ray Eberle singing. Etta James’s definitive version came later, on Argo, in 1960.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: This one runs backwards from the usual pattern. Most eclipsed originals are obscure records that a later star found and outsang; here the original was made by the biggest band in America, and it still lost. Part of the reason is that “At Last” was mishandled from the start — Gordon and Warren wrote it for Sun Valley Serenade in 1941, and Darryl Zanuck decided the picture had too many big numbers and cut the vocal out of the release print. The song sat unheard while Miller’s orchestra made studio recordings of it in 1941 that were never issued. When the vocal arrangement was finally revived for Orchestra Wives and recorded properly in May 1942, it went out as a B-side, and the label on the disc credited the second film rather than the one it was written for.

Then the window shut. Miller’s recording was made before the American Federation of Musicians’ recording ban began at midnight on July 31, 1942, and the band itself stopped existing that September when Miller went into the Army. There was no follow-up, no re-cut, no long tail of the orchestra reinterpreting its own hit. The song sat as a wartime artifact until Ray Anthony — who had played trumpet in that very orchestra, and who as of 2026 is its last surviving member — remade it in 1952 to the highest US chart placing the song has ever had. Etta James came to it as material with no living owner, and her reading was so complete that it stopped sounding like an interpretation of anything.
context.detailsSummary: The full chronology, step by step
detailsBody: 1941 — Mack Gordon and Harry Warren write “At Last” for the 20th Century-Fox musical Sun Valley Serenade. It is filmed with Glenn Miller’s orchestra, John Payne and Lynn Bari, whose singing is dubbed by Pat Friday. Studio head Darryl Zanuck cuts the vocal from the release print; only instrumental passages survive in the finished film.
1941 — Miller’s orchestra makes studio recordings of the song. None of them are released.

May 20, 1942 — The orchestra records it again in Hollywood, with Ray Eberle singing and an arrangement by Jerry Gray and Bill Finegan. Victor logs it as matrix PBS-072285; take one becomes the master. Harry Meyerson supervises the session.
July 10, 1942 — Released by RCA Victor as catalogue 27934, the B-side of “(I’ve Got a Gal in) Kalamazoo.” The label credits the film Orchestra Wives, in which the vocal arrangement was reused.
Midnight, July 31, 1942 — The American Federation of Musicians’ recording ban begins; union musicians can no longer make commercial recordings. It runs until November 11, 1944.

August 1942 — The record charts. Wikipedia’s cited data has it entering Billboard’s radio-plug listing at number 17 on August 1 and peaking at number two on August 29; other reference sources report lower peaks, and this page does not treat any single figure as settled.
September 27, 1942 — Miller’s civilian orchestra plays its last concert, in Passaic, New Jersey, and disbands as he enters military service.
October 1943 — The 1942 recording is pressed as a U.S. Army V-Disc, No. 12A, for distribution to troops.
1952 — Ray Anthony and His Orchestra, led by a former Miller trumpeter, reach number two on Billboard’s pop singles chart with a remake — the highest-charting American version of the song.
November 15, 1960 — Etta James releases At Last! on Argo Records, produced by Leonard and Phil Chess, with the title track arranged by Riley Hampton.
April 1961 — Her single reaches number two on the R&B chart and number 47 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1999 — The Etta James recording is inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
context.pull: The song everyone plays at weddings started life as the flip side of a novelty number about Kalamazoo.

listen.what: The original 1942 recording — Glenn Miller and His Orchestra with Ray Eberle, digitised directly from the RCA Victor 27934-B shellac disc, surface noise and all.
listen.source: Not a fan upload or a rip: this is a library digitisation from the Internet Archive’s Great 78 Project, transferred and restored by George Blood, L.P. Identity was confirmed against the physical artifact rather than by ear — the item metadata carries catalogue number 27934-B and the matrix stamp 27934B, which match the Victor ledger entry for matrix PBS-072285 (May 20, 1942, Hollywood, take one, issued on Victor 27934) and the MusicBrainz release for RCA Victor 27934. There is no re-recording risk here, because the object being played is the 1942 pressing itself. Note that MusicBrainz carries no duration for this recording, so the usual duration cross-check was unavailable; the Archive item reports a runtime of 3:12.

listenCover.what: Etta James’ 1960 Argo recording, the title track of At Last! and the version everyone means by the song.

Runtime 180s (3:00), matching the MusicBrainz “At Last (mono version)” recording on At Last! dated 1960-11-15 at 3:00, and within a second of the 3:01 stereo entry from the same release.
